Day 3: Estimation, comparison and regression

Confidence intervals, bivariate tests, linear and logistic regression

Adamu Onu

NexusHealth

Where we are

You bring

  • the analysis set (522 patients)
  • your framework map (which variables are confounders?)
  • your hypotheses

Today you will produce

  • a bivariate comparison with an effect size and 95% CI
  • an adjusted linear model with a diagnostic note

Block 1: Estimation and choosing a method

Start with the estimand

Among adults in primary care, how much does mean systolic BP differ per 10-point higher adherence score, among patients of the same age, sex, BMI, diabetes status and smoking status?

It fixes four things before any test is run:

  • the population (adults in primary care)
  • the contrast (per 10 points of adherence)
  • the outcome scale (mean SBP in mmHg)
  • the adjustment set (from the framework)

Confidence intervals and p-values

95% confidence interval

The range of values for the true effect that are reasonably compatible with the data.

Width shows precision. Narrow means precise, not important.

p-value

How surprising the data would be if there were truly no effect.

It is not the probability that H0 is true, and it says nothing about the size of the effect.

Always report the effect size with its 95% CI. Add the p-value if you like. Then judge clinical importance yourself.

Example: mean SBP

Mean SBP in the analysis set: 141.3 mmHg (95% CI 140.4 to 142.1; n = 522)

  • Estimate: 141.3
  • Standard error: SD / √n = 10.0 / √522 ≈ 0.44
  • 95% CI: estimate ± about 2 standard errors

More patients means a smaller standard error, and so a narrower interval.

Choosing a method

Outcome Exposure Bivariate method Effect measure Model
Continuous Two groups Welch t-test Difference in means Linear regression
Continuous Continuous Correlation Pearson r / Spearman ρ Linear regression
Binary Categories Chi-square Difference in proportions Logistic regression
Binary Continuous (go straight to a model) Odds ratio Logistic regression

Choose the method

Notebook 03, Part A. Individually, then compare, 20 minutes.

For each question name the outcome type, exposure type, bivariate method and effect measure:

  1. Is mean BMI different between current and never smokers?
  2. Does the proportion with uncontrolled BP differ between clinics?
  3. Is adherence associated with uncontrolled BP after allowing for age and diabetes?

Then write H0, H1 and the effect measure for your own question.

Block 2: Bivariate analysis

Comparing two means: Welch t-test

  1. Describe: group sizes, means, SDs.
  2. Picture: a boxplot.
  3. Estimate: the difference in means with 95% CI.
  4. Test: Welch’s t-test (does not assume equal variances).
Diabetes n Mean SBP (SD)
No 393 140.4 (10.1)
Yes 129 143.7 (9.4)

Difference 3.3 mmHg (95% CI 1.4 to 5.2), p < 0.001. Clear statistically; modest clinically; unadjusted.

Comparing proportions: chi-square

Smoking Controlled Uncontrolled % uncontrolled
Never 80 189 70.3
Former 57 104 64.6
Current 27 65 70.7

χ² = 1.72, df = 2, p = 0.42. Smallest expected count 28.9 (all above 5, so the test is reliable).

A large p-value is not evidence of no difference. It means the data are compatible with a range of differences, including none.

Correlation

Adherence and SBP: Pearson r = -0.13 (p = 0.003)

  • Weak: adherence explains under 2% of SBP variation.
  • Still potentially important at a population level.
  • Plot first. r only describes straight-line relationships.
  • Correlation cannot adjust for confounders.
r Rough description
0 to 0.1 Negligible
0.1 to 0.3 Weak
0.3 to 0.5 Moderate
above 0.5 Strong

Defend a bivariate analysis

Notebook 03, Part B. In pairs, 60 minutes.

  1. Exercise 3A part 1: SBP by diabetes. Summaries, boxplot, Welch test, difference with 95% CI.
  2. Exercise 3A part 2: uncontrolled BP by diabetes. Cross-table, chi-square, difference in proportions.
  3. Interpret each in one or two sentences, plus one limitation.

AI assist: ask Copilot to explain the test output line by line, then confirm which group was subtracted from which. Getting the direction wrong is a very common error.

Block 3: Linear regression

What linear regression estimates

SBP = intercept + b1 × adherence_10 + b2 × age + ... + error

  • b1: difference in mean SBP per 10-point higher adherence, among people with the same values of the other variables.
  • Categories are compared with a reference level (Female; Never smoker; no diabetes).
  • Adjust for confounders from your framework. Do not adjust for mediators or colliders.

Crude and adjusted

Model Adherence (per 10 points), mmHg 95% CI p
Crude -0.76 -1.25 to -0.27 0.003
Adjusted -1.01 -1.49 to -0.53 < 0.001

Adjusted for age, sex, BMI, diabetes and smoking; n = 522.

The estimate grew after adjustment. Something we adjusted for was masking part of the association (negative confounding). Adjustment can move an estimate in either direction.

Reading the other coefficients

Term Estimate (mmHg) 95% CI Reads as
Age (per year) 0.17 0.11 to 0.23 Each year older: 0.17 mmHg higher
BMI (per kg/m²) 0.28 0.11 to 0.45 Each unit of BMI: 0.28 mmHg higher
Current smoker 2.77 0.49 to 5.04 Compared with never smokers
Male 0.50 -1.16 to 2.16 Compared with females; CI includes 0

Report only what answers your question. The covariates are there to adjust, not to be interpreted one by one.

Check the assumptions

No funnel, no curve, Q-Q close to the line: the model looks reasonable. R² ≈ 0.11, so most SBP variation is unexplained, which is common.

Fit, check and interpret a linear model

Notebook 03, Part C. In pairs, 60 minutes.

  1. Fit the crude model and read the adherence coefficient.
  2. Exercise 3B: fit the adjusted model; compare crude and adjusted estimates in a small table.
  3. Make the diagnostic plots and write a two-sentence diagnostic note.
  4. Interpret the adjusted estimate in one sentence a colleague could read.

Done when: two-model comparison, adjusted estimate with CI, diagnostic note.

Block 4: Logistic regression

Probability, odds and odds ratios

Scale Definition Example
Probability (risk) Share with the outcome 0.69
Odds p / (1 - p) 0.69 / 0.31 = 2.2
Odds ratio (OR) Odds in one group ÷ odds in another 0.81

Logistic regression models the log-odds. Exponentiate a coefficient to get an OR.

OR = 1: no association. OR < 1: lower odds. OR > 1: higher odds.

Odds are not risks

With a common outcome (69% here), the OR exaggerates the change in risk.

Adherence score Average predicted probability of uncontrolled BP
40 78%
60 71%
80 62%

Adjusted OR per 10 points: 0.81 (95% CI 0.72 to 0.91). “19% lower odds” is correct. “19% lower risk” is wrong.

Use predicted probabilities when you want to talk about risk.

Write a defensible logistic interpretation

Notebook 03, Part D. In pairs, 60 minutes.

  1. Fit the crude and adjusted logistic models.
  2. Exercise 3C: odds ratios with 95% CIs; average predicted probability at adherence 40, 60 and 80.
  3. Write three sentences: the adjusted OR with its CI, what it means, and what the predicted probabilities add.
  4. Save the model results for Day 4.

AI assist: ask your assistant to critique your three sentences for odds/risk confusion and causal language. Accept only changes you can justify.

  • a bivariate comparison with an effect size, 95% CI and limitation
  • crude and adjusted linear estimates with a diagnostic note
  • an adjusted OR, predicted probabilities and a three-sentence interpretation
  • outputs/tables/model_results.csv
